metadata.title: From Syntactic Inversion to Literary, Archetypal Inversion: Toward a New Figure of Thought in Literary Theory
metadata.description:
Abstract:

Stylistic Inversion represents a figure of thought that is traditionally treated in school curricula and stylistic manuals as a syntactic figure: a deviation from ordinary word order used for emphasis, rhythm, poetic musicality, rhyme, or archaic elevation. In this conventional sense, inversion belongs primarily to grammar, syntax, and prosody. This article proposes a broader literary-theoretical distinction between syntactic inversion and literary inversion, the latter understood as a macro-structural figure of thought through which inherited roles, archetypes, burdens, actions, or symbolic destinies are reversed, exchanged, or reassigned in order to produce a new moral, social, theological, or existential meaning. While syntactic inversion rearranges words, literary inversion rearranges symbolic functions and inherited destinies. Figuratively, a literary inversion may be as necessary as a mountain switchback road, climbing to the summit of knowledge, wisdom and illumination in the domains of literary theory and creative writing.

The paper defines literary inversion as a conceptual and archetypal mechanism rather than a merely grammatical one. It distinguishes the proposed concept from related categories such as subversion, parody, chiasmus, intertextuality, mythic rewriting, and structural reversal, while acknowledging that literary inversion may overlap with these procedures in specific texts. Several subtypes are proposed, including archetypal inversion, mythological inversion, gendered inversion, historical inversion, and soteriological inversion. These subtypes allow the concept to be applied flexibly across mythopoetic, theological, feminist, intertextual, and philosophical literature.

As a case study, the article examines Andromeda: A New Stellar (Re-)Genesis – A Poem That Does Not End, where the figures of Andromeda, Sophia, the New Adam, and the New Eve enact a reciprocal reversal of Genesis-based roles. In the poem, the Andromeda man symbolically enters birth-giving pain, the Sophia woman enters labouring struggle, the New Adam carries the Cross of the New Eve, the New Eve carries the Cross of the New Adam, and the apple of death is inverted into a breath of life. The Fall is therefore not merely repeated as inherited blame, but transformed into a symbolic structure of mutual restoration. The Andromeda epic poem manuscript is available online, also as the Supplementary Materials for the present study.

With regards to the main theme and literary motifs of the poem, the most important type of literary inversion in the case study regarding the Andromeda epic poem is gender inversion, which starts from its title, given that the original mythic story of Andromeda involves a trapped Princess named Andromeda, who was rescued by a Prince. In Theodor-Nicolae Carp's "Andromeda" poem, the main character's name is Andromeda and he is presented as a male figure, namely a Prince from a different human archetype who emerged in a cosmic place far from the Earth, who eventually becomes trapped in the prison of mediocrity and mortality pushed by the "Milk-Made", Earthly human civilisation, before he is rescued and revived by a female character, an Earthly figure named Sophia who becomes the main female character. Sophia, whose initial name was 'Miley-Kasey' and who represented a strong reliance for the power and influence of the "Milk-Made" mediocrity, had hidden aspirations toward the absolute and who suddenly "betrayed" the dark Prince of mediocrity, by choosing the absolute over the relative and escaping their palace to encounter and offer Andromeda respect, care and real, unconditional love. Likewise, Theodor Carp's Andromeda epic poem offers an alternative story ending to Mihai Eminescu's "Luceafarul" ("The Morning Star") poem.

Hence, the article argues that literary inversion may become a useful analytical and pedagogical concept for high school and university literary study, especially in discussions of mythopoetic literature, theological symbolism, gender reconciliation, and modern rewritings of foundational narratives. If syntactic inversion teaches students how poetry rearranges words, literary inversion teaches them how literature rearranges wounded histories.

data.title: From Syntactic Inversion to Literary, Archetypal Inversion: Toward a New Figure of Thought in Literary Theory

metadata.title: Eve at The Petit Palais, Paris
metadata.description: Eve is an early piece of work by sculptor Aimé-Jules Dalou (Paris, 1838-1902), notably known for his public monuments. He took heavy influence from Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux (11 May 1827 – 12 October 1875) mentioned here, Eve is represented as a graceful adolescent, kneeling in a pose similar to 'Pecheur a la coquille' (also by Jules Dalou, also uploaded to Scan The World from The Petit Palais). The snake crawling up the side of ther leg justifies the biblical title, signifying the charming of the girl.     This object is part of Scan The World. metadata.title: Adam and Eve: Eve
metadata.description: The statue of our forebears formed part of Bandinelli's sculptural project for the choir stalls of the Florentine Duomo, initiated in 1542.  Completed in 1551, the figures were separated from the Tree of Wisdom in wood and stucco, which was destroyed in the flood of 1966, just like the original base. In 1722, the group was removed from the choir stalls due to the nudity of the figures, considered obscene. It was initially moved to the Uffizi, and subsequently to the Bargello.   The matching statue of Adam can be downloaded here.     This object is part of Scan The World. metadata.title: Eve
metadata.description: Eve is a figure in the Book of Genesis in the Hebrew Bible. According to the creation myth of the Abrahamic religions, she was the first woman. In Islamic tradition, Eve is known as Adam's wife and the first woman although she is not specifically named in the Quran.  According to the second chapter of Genesis, Eve was created by God (Yahweh) by taking her from the rib of Adam, to be Adam's companion. She succumbs to the serpent's temptation to eat the forbidden fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. She shares the fruit with Adam, and as a result the first humans are expelled from the Garden of Eden. Christian churches differ on how they view both Adam and Eve's disobedience to God (often called the fall of man), and to the consequences that those actions had on the rest of humanity. Christian and Jewish teachings sometimes hold Adam (the first man) and Eve to a different level of responsibility for the fall, although Islamicteaching holds both equally responsible.  Although Eve is not a saint's name, the traditional name day of Adam and Eve has been celebrated on December 24 since the Middle Ages in many European countries such as Germany, Hungary, Scandinavia, Estonia, and Lithuania.     This object is part of Scan The World. metadata.title: O Indio E A Suassuapara
metadata.description: Victor Brecheret, born Vittorio Breheret (December 15, 1894 – December 17, 1955), was an Italian-Brazilian sculptor. He lived most of his life in São Paulo, except for his studies in Paris in his early twenties. Brecheret's work combines techniques of European modernist sculpture with references to his native country through the physical characteristics of his human forms and visual motifs drawn from Brazilian folk art. Many of his subjects are figures from the Bible or classical mythology.  Brecheret was one of the first Brazilian modernists to achieve success. In 1921 his sculpture Eve was acquired by the São Paulo city hall. In 1922 his work was exhibited in the foyer of the Municipal Theatre during the Week of Modern Art (Semana de Arte Moderna). His O Grup was acquired by the French government in 1934 for the Musée du Jeu de Paume; it was later moved to the public library at La Roche-sur-Yon, where it remains on display. His best-known work, the massive Monumento às Bandeiras at the Parque Ibirapuera in São Paulo, was proposed (in the form of a plaster miniature) in 1920, begun in 1936, and completed on January 25, 1953. metadata.title: Eve Before Sin
metadata.description: Eugene Delaplanche completed two works on the subject of the Bible's first woman. The more famous of the two is Eve After the Fall (1869) but he followed it up with Eve before the fall (1891)   The work began with a wax sketch and a plaster cast but was soon made into a marble statue whihc arrived at the Musee D'Orsay after stays in Luxembourg and the Louvre

metadata.title: The Devil's Hand
metadata.description: A large left hand emerges from a solid block holding a human figure in a contracted position.  This piece appears to be a complementary one to "The Hand of God" by the same artist, Rodin. This last one representing a right hand emerging from a marble block and holding two human figures, Adam and Eve.  The Hand of Devil, represents the perfect link to a series of works made by the artist during the 1890s, such as "The Cathedral" and "The Secret".
